summary: A space-vocabulary/naming topic for ages 5–8: learn the eight planets in order from the Sun and the core space nouns (planet, star, sun, moon, satellite, orbit, solar system, galaxy, universe, asteroid, comet), and use them correctly to describe what is in the sky. Anchor each word to a canonical image plus one defining feature, lock in planet order with a mnemonic and ordering practice, build the load-bearing verb 'orbit' (what goes round what), and explicitly separate confusable categories — the Sun is a star (not a planet), the Moon is a satellite (not a planet), stars make their own light while planets shine by reflected light. Keep the focus on naming and correct use; defer mechanisms (why things orbit, phases) to later topics.
misconceptions: The Sun is a planet (it is a star) — or, conversely, the Sun is not a star at all.
The Moon is a planet, rather than a satellite orbiting Earth.
Stars and planets are the same, and a 'shooting star' (a meteor) is a star.
Pluto is still the ninth planet — it was reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006.
Planets are all similar in size and packed close together, a scale error picked up from diagrams.

activities.title: Tap-through solar-system scene with category badges
steps: Explore a single richly labelled solar-system scene where tapping each body reveals its name, one memorable feature, and a category badge: planet / star / moon / asteroid / comet.
Tap the Sun to lift a flap that declares 'I'm a star, not a planet'.
Use a lift-the-flap that contrasts how a moon differs from a planet (a moon — also called a natural satellite — orbits a planet; a planet orbits the Sun).
Tap a comet to reveal its name and its defining feature — an icy body that grows a glowing tail when it comes near the Sun — so every target word has a picture-and-feature anchor.
Follow a zoom-out drill-down that travels outward: solar system → Milky Way galaxy → universe, so the nesting words land as places you move out through.
Tap two look-alike dots in a night-sky panel; the panel reveals that one is a planet (shines by borrowed, reflected light) and the other a star (makes its own light).
activities.insight: Each space word belongs to a specific kind of object, and the key distinction the whole vocabulary hinges on — a star makes its own light, a planet shines by reflected light — is made clear through the tap-reveal comparison of two look-alike dots; it is not something a child can simply judge by eye.

activities.title: Order the planets and sort sky objects
steps: Drag the eight planets into correct order outward from the Sun (Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune), using a mnemonic such as 'My Very Easy Method Just Speeds Up Naming' as a memory aid.

Sort a set of sky objects into bins by category: makes its own light (star), a big, round world that orbits the Sun and shines by borrowed light (planet), orbits a planet (moon), a small rocky body that orbits the Sun, often lumpy in shape (asteroid).
Repeat the ordering until the sequence is secure.
activities.insight: Naming the eight planets in order and placing each sky object in the right category are the two headline skills, rehearsed through active placement with feedback.

activities.title: Build the nested 'orbit' idea with hands and narration
steps: Show 'orbit' with a hand — move one fist around another and say what is going around what.
Narrate the nesting: the Moon orbits the Earth; the planets orbit the Sun (a star); the solar system sits within a galaxy, within the universe.

Answer probe questions: 'Is the Sun a planet, or something else?'; 'What does the Moon orbit — the Earth or the Sun?' (it orbits the Earth, and travels around the Sun together with the Earth); 'If I said Mars is a moon, would that be right? Why not?'
activities.insight: 'Orbit' means travelling around, not being near or next to — and the going-around relationships are nested (moon→planet, planet→Sun).

checkQuestion: Here's a picture of the Sun with lots of things around it. Walk me from the Sun outwards and tell me the story of our solar system — point to each thing, tell me what it is and how it moves.
checkAnswer: In running speech the child names the planets Mercury→Neptune in order, uses 'orbit' for the going-around motion (planets orbit the Sun; the Moon orbits the Earth), calls the Sun a star, a satellite a 'moon', and applies 'asteroid' correctly — reserving each term for the right object rather than reciting definitions.
